result.summary: Pausanias travels past the Alpheus through Trapezus and Bathos, where the Arcadians place the battle of gods and giants. He argues from Homer and from a huge coffin found in Syria that giants were mortal men, then describes the ruined towns of Basilis and Thocnia.

scenes.title: Bathos and the Giants' Battle
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the district of Trapezus and Bathos, with its rites, spring and fire. The Arcadians claim the battle of gods and giants happened here.

scenes.title: Were the Giants Mortal?
scenes.summary: Pausanias cites Homer to show giants were mortal and dismisses the dragon-feet fable. He tells of the giant coffin found when the Orontes was diverted.

scenes.title: Basilis and Thocnia
scenes.summary: Pausanias notes the ruined towns of Basilis and Thocnia and the rivers near them.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias's rationalizing argument that India, producing huge beasts, would also produce giant humans.

analysis.text: Pausanias rationalizes myth, turning giants into large mortal men and supporting this with Homer and physical evidence.
Finds of huge bones were commonly explained in antiquity as heroes or giants, and local claims tied Greek myths to specific places.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias's giant coffin story shows how ancient writers interpreted fossil or large bone discoveries as remains of heroes.

language_notes.text: The Great Goddesses are Demeter and Persephone (Kore), honored in Arcadia with mystery rites.
Pallene in Thrace (the Chalcidic peninsula) was the usual Greek location for the Gigantomachy, the gods' battle with the giants.
The Læstrygones were man-eating giants in the Odyssey; the Phæacian king is Alcinous, who compares his people's closeness to the gods.
Greek laos can mean 'people' or 'host'; Pausanias argues it implies many individuals, hence mortal men, not a single divine line.
A cubit was roughly the length of a forearm, about 18 inches, so the coffin was over 16 feet long.
Clarus, near Colophon, had a famous oracle of Apollo, which Syrians consulted about the find.
A stade was a Greek unit of length, about 600 feet (roughly 180 metres).

context_notes.text: The Orontes flows through Syria past Antioch; the Emperor is a Roman one, unnamed here.
Cresphontes was one of the Heraclidae who took the Peloponnese and received Messenia; Cypselus was an Arcadian king.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias speaks as a skeptical, rationalizing traveller, weighing myth against evidence and dismissing the dragon-footed giants.
Pausanias poses his argument about India as a question, presenting his conclusion as obvious while using natural philosophy to explain the giant's size.
